name: Daui
sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Two minor figures of Irish legend share the name Daui. The first was Daui Dalta Dedad, a king of Tara. He kept his brother from the throne by blinding him. A king with a blemish could not rule, so the injury was an effective tool. Daui won power this way, but he held it only seven years. He was assassinated soon after. The second figure was Daui Ladrach, a king of similar ambition. He too was willing to kill to gain the throne. The warrior Lugaidh Laíghde proved the cleverer of the two. He used Daui's ambition to clear his own path to power. For the first figure the dictionary gives Daui Dalta Dedad and Daui Dallta Dedad as spellings. Duach Dallta Deadad stands beside them. The Irish name means Blinder of Dedad. One variant makes him Dedad's foster-son, his dalta, instead of his brother. Medieval redactors tried to date his assassination to the same hour as that of Julius Caesar. The second figure appears as Daui Ladrach, Duach Ladrach, Ladgrach, or Laghrach, from an Irish word for crooked-toed or splay-footed. He was the son of Fiachu Tolgrach. To gain the throne he killed Airgetmar. Lugaid Laigde later betrayed him, though Lugaid had helped in the ousting. Airgetmar's grandson Aed Ruad in time killed Lugaid and took the kingship himself.

okr.objective: Two kings named Daui, and how each ambition failed or fell to a cleverer rival, illustrates the cost of the throne in Irish legend.
key_results: Daui Dalta Dedad was a king of Tara who blinded his brother.
A blemished king could not rule, so blinding secured the throne.
Daui Dalta Dedad was assassinated after only seven years.
Daui Ladrach fell to the warrior Lugaidh Laíghde.
